title: Work and Jobs
overview: This is the first A2 unit, and the jump is real: from saying what you do to saying what a job requires, what it does not require, and how much of it you have to do. That distinction — must do it, do not have to do it — is where obligation goes wrong in English, and getting it backwards at work is expensive. The unit ends with a real contract, because the conditions that matter to you are rarely the ones printed largest.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 has a trap in it — read the worked example twice.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a contract and a job advertisement.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is the one that separates the two meanings.
Record yourself describing a job and explaining what it requires.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
This unit contains one of the few places in English where getting a word slightly wrong reverses your meaning completely, so we are going to spend most of the lesson on it.
The pattern is have to. It means something is necessary — a rule, a requirement, a condition of the job.
I have to start at eight. She has to wear a uniform. We have to work one weekend a month.
Notice has to for he, she and it. That is the third-person -s from Unit 3, doing its normal job on a new verb. Nothing new there.
And because have is a normal verb, the question and the negative use do and does, exactly as in Unit 5.
Do I have to work on Saturday? Does she have to wear a uniform?
Now the trap, and it is the whole reason this pattern gets its own card.
Do not have to does NOT mean must not.
It means it is not necessary. There is no rule. You may, if you want to.
You do not have to wear a uniform. That means: no uniform is required. Wear one if you like. Nobody minds.
Compare that with: You must not wear a uniform. That means: a uniform is forbidden.
Those are opposite meanings, and they are one word apart. Must not is a closed door. Do not have to is an open one.
Most learners meet must not and do not have to in the same lesson somewhere and never fully separate them. We are separating them by keeping them apart: this unit owns have to, and must and must not belong to Unit 17. Here, all you need is that do not have to means it is not necessary. Nothing is forbidden in this unit.
One memory line, and it is worth keeping: do not have to is a permission, not a prohibition.
Second pattern: describing what a job involves. This is not new grammar. It is the present simple from Unit 5 and third-person -s from Unit 3, put to a particular use, and the difficulty is not the tense — it is knowing what to say.
A good job description has three parts, and people usually only give the first.
What you do: I deal with customers. She manages a team of six.
What the job requires: You have to be reliable. You have to work quickly.
What it is like: It is quite hard work. It is really interesting.
The first part alone is a job title with extra words. All three together is a description.
And notice the verb involves, which does a lot of work here: the job involves a lot of walking. Involves means includes as a necessary part. It is one of the most useful verbs in this whole area.
Third pattern: adverbs of degree. These are the small words that go before an adjective and change how much.
Very, which you met in Unit 4. Quite, which is less than very. And really, which is more than very and much more common in speech than most courses admit.
It is quite hard. Less than very hard.
It is very hard.
It is really hard. More than very.
So the scale is: quite, then very, then really.
One warning about quite, because it will confuse you at some point. In this course quite means fairly, a moderate amount — quite good means fairly good, and it is a smaller claim than very good. Some speakers use quite to mean completely, especially with words like right and finished. When you hear quite and it does not seem to mean fairly, that is what has happened. You do not need to produce that use. You only need to recognise that it exists.
And the word order never changes: the degree word goes immediately before the adjective. Really interesting. Quite difficult. Very tired. Never after.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: Not Required Is Not Forbidden
readings.passage:
There is one confusion in English that costs people real opportunities, and it happens at the moment they are least able to check.
You do not have to have experience.
Read that again. It means experience is not required. Apply anyway. You are welcome.
Many people read it as though it said something closer to you should not have experience, or they read the whole sentence quickly, see experience and a negative, and decide the job is not for them. Then they do not apply.
The rule is simple and worth memorising as a sentence rather than as a grammar point. Do not have to means it is not necessary. It never means it is not allowed.
Job advertisements are full of this construction, and almost always it is opening a door rather than closing one.
You do not have to have a qualification.
You do not have to work weekends.
You do not have to have your own transport.
Every one of those is good news. Every one of them is telling you that a thing you might have worried about does not matter.
The reverse construction — the one that does close a door — uses different words entirely, and you will meet it in Unit 17. In this unit, every negative you see is an open door. If you read one and feel discouraged, read it again more slowly, because you have almost certainly read it backwards.

readings.title: Describing a Job in Three Parts
readings.passage:
Ask someone what their job is and most people give you a title. I work in a shop. I am a driver. That is accurate and it tells the listener almost nothing.
A description has three parts, and each answers a different question.
What you actually do. Not the title — the activity. I serve customers and I organise the deliveries. I drive a van and I deliver to about twenty shops a day. This is the part people can picture.
What the job requires. This is where have to belongs. You have to be reliable. You have to start at six. You have to be quite good with numbers. This is the part that tells someone whether they could do it.
What it is like. It is quite hard work. The team is really good. It is more interesting than it sounds. This is the part that tells someone whether they would want to.
The three parts do different work and leaving one out has a predictable effect. Without the first, you have said nothing concrete. Without the second, nobody can judge whether they could do it. Without the third, it sounds like a contract rather than a life.
One small thing that improves any description. Use the verb involves. The job involves a lot of walking. It involves working alone most of the day. Involves means includes as a necessary part, and it lets you name something that is neither a duty nor an opinion — just a fact about what the work is actually like.

readings.title: The Advertisement, and What the Contract Says
readings.setting: A job advertisement in a window, and the contract offered afterwards.
readings.passage:
WAREHOUSE ASSISTANT
  Northfield Distribution

  30 hours per week
  GBP 11.60 per hour

  · No experience necessary
  · Full training given
  · You do not have to have your own
    transport - free staff bus from the
    station

  Apply online by 30 September.
  Two references required.

-----------------------------------------

  CONTRACT OF EMPLOYMENT - EXTRACT

  3.1  Normal hours are 30 per week,
       worked over 4 or 5 days as the
       employer requires.

  3.2  Employees may be required to work
       up to 8 hours' overtime per week.
       Overtime is paid at the normal
       hourly rate.

  4.1  Holiday entitlement is 28 days,
       including public holidays.

  4.2  Holiday may not be taken during
       November or December.

  6.1  Notice period: 1 week during the
       first 3 months, 4 weeks thereafter.

  6.2  The first 3 months are a trial
       period. Either side may end the
       contract with 1 week's notice.

comprehension.q: What does you do not have to have experience mean?
comprehension.a: Experience is not required — you are welcome to apply without it.
comprehension.why: It opens a door. This is the single most important sentence in the unit and the one most often read backwards.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say this confusion costs people opportunities?
comprehension.a: Because they read the negative as discouraging, decide the job is not for them, and do not apply — when the sentence was telling them a worry did not matter.
comprehension.why: The cost is not a mark on an exercise. It is a job not applied for, and the person never finds out.

comprehension.q: The text says every negative in this unit is an open door. What is it preparing you for?
comprehension.a: Unit 17, where the construction that does close a door uses different words entirely.
comprehension.why: The two are kept in separate units on purpose. Knowing that a closing form exists, but is not here, stops you from reading one into these sentences.

comprehension.q: What are the three parts of a job description?
comprehension.a: What you actually do, what the job requires, and what it is like.
comprehension.why: Each answers a different question, and most people give only the first — which is a title with extra words.

comprehension.q: What happens if you leave out the third part?
comprehension.a: It sounds like a contract rather than a life — the listener cannot tell whether they would want the job.
comprehension.why: The text gives a specific consequence for each missing part, and this is the one people leave out most, because opinions feel less safe than facts.

comprehension.q: Why does the text recommend the verb involves?
comprehension.a: Because it lets you name something that is neither a duty nor an opinion — just a fact about what the work is actually like.
comprehension.why: It fills a gap the other two parts leave. A lot of walking is not a requirement and not a judgement, but it is the thing a listener most wants to know.

comprehension.q: The advertisement says you do not have to have your own transport. What does that tell you, and what does it not tell you?
comprehension.a: It tells you transport is not required and there is a free staff bus from the station. It does not tell you what times the bus runs, which matters if your shift starts early.
comprehension.why: The open door is real, but it has a condition attached that the advertisement does not state. Noticing what is absent is the harder half of reading a document.

comprehension.q: Do you have to do overtime in this job?
comprehension.a: You may be required to — clause 3.2 says employees may be required to work up to 8 hours a week. So it is not optional, and it is paid at the normal rate rather than a higher one.
comprehension.why: Two facts sit in one short clause, and the second is the one that costs money. Overtime is often paid at a higher rate; here it is not, and only the contract says so.

comprehension.q: You want to take a week's holiday in December. Can you?
comprehension.a: No. Clause 4.2 says holiday may not be taken during November or December.
comprehension.why: This is the one restriction in the whole document, and it is in the contract rather than the advertisement — which is normal, and the reason for reading one before signing.

comprehension.q: You start the job and leave after two months. How much notice do you have to give, and why is that different from later?
comprehension.a: One week, because the first three months are a trial period. After three months it becomes four weeks.
comprehension.why: Clauses 6.1 and 6.2 say the same thing from two directions. The short notice cuts both ways — it is easier for you to leave and easier for them to end it.

grammar.title: Have to: what the job requires
grammar.explanation: Have to means something is necessary — a rule, a requirement, a condition. The form is ordinary: it takes third-person -s from Unit 3, and questions and negatives use do and does exactly as in Unit 5.
grammar.rule:
POSITIVE
  I / you / we / they  have to  start at eight.
  he / she / it        has to   wear a uniform.

QUESTION
  Do I have to work on Saturday?
  Does she have to wear a uniform?

NEGATIVE — read this carefully
  You do not have to wear a uniform.
  = it is NOT NECESSARY. Wear one if you like.

  It does NOT mean a uniform is forbidden.
  That is a different form, and it is Unit 17.

DO NOT HAVE TO  =  an open door.
grammar.workedExample:
A job advertisement says: you do not have to have experience. Should you apply?
1. Find the structure: do not have to.
2. Ask what it means: it is not necessary.
3. So experience is not required. Nothing is forbidden.
4. Result: yes — apply. The sentence is good news.
Now the reverse. You want to ask whether weekend work is required.
1. It is a question about necessity, so use have to.
2. Questions take do: Do I have to work at weekends?
3. If the answer is you do not have to, weekends are optional.
The test that never fails: replace do not have to with it is not necessary to and read the sentence again. If it still makes sense, you have understood it correctly.
grammar.mistake: Reading do not have to as a prohibition. You do not have to wear a uniform means no uniform is required, not that uniforms are banned. This reverses the meaning of the sentence and, in a job advertisement, turns an invitation into a rejection. The other error is dropping to: I have work on Saturday. Have to is two words and both are needed.
grammar.tip: Do not have to means it is not necessary. It never means it is not allowed.
grammar.practice:
Write have to, has to, do not have to or does not have to.
1. I ____ start at eight every morning.
2. She ____ wear a uniform — it is a rule.
3. You ____ have experience. Anyone can apply.
4. He ____ give four weeks' notice.
5. We ____ work weekends. It is optional.
6. ____ I ____ bring anything to the interview?
grammar.answers:
1. have to
2. has to
3. do not have to
4. has to
5. do not have to
6. Do … have to
Numbers 3 and 5 are the ones to check. Both mean it is not necessary — anyone can apply, and weekends are optional. Neither forbids anything.
Number 2 and number 4 both use has to because she and he are third person. That is the Unit 3 -s doing its ordinary job.

grammar.title: Describing what a job involves
grammar.explanation: No new grammar — this is the present simple from Unit 5 and have to from card 1, put to a particular use. The difficulty is not the tense. It is knowing what to say, and there are exactly three parts.
grammar.rule:
1  WHAT YOU DO      (present simple)
     I serve customers and organise the deliveries.

2  WHAT IT REQUIRES  (have to)
     You have to be reliable.
     You have to start at six.

3  WHAT IT IS LIKE   (adverb of degree)
     It is quite hard work.
     The team is really good.

AND ONE USEFUL VERB:
  involves = includes as a necessary part
     The job involves a lot of walking.
     It involves working alone most of the day.
grammar.workedExample:
Describe a delivery job.
1. Part one — what you actually do, not the title: I drive a van and I deliver to about twenty shops a day.
2. Part two — what it requires, using have to: You have to start at six, and you have to be reliable.
3. Part three — what it is like, using a degree word: It is quite hard work, but it is really interesting because you are not in one place all day.
4. Add an involves sentence for the fact that is neither duty nor opinion: The job involves a lot of driving.
Put together, that is four sentences and a listener now knows what you do, whether they could do it, and whether they would want to.
Compare with what most people say: I am a driver. Same job, and the listener knows nothing.
grammar.mistake: Giving the title and stopping. I work in a shop is not a description — it is a category. The other common gap is leaving out part three, because saying what a job is like feels like an opinion and opinions feel risky. It is the part that tells someone whether they would want the job, and without it the description sounds like a contract.
grammar.tip: What you do, what it requires, what it is like. All three, every time.
grammar.practice:
Describe each job in three parts. One sentence per part.
1. Working in a shop.
2. Driving a delivery van.
3. Supervising a small team.
4. A job you have done, or would like to do.
grammar.answers:
Model answers — yours will differ, and should.
1. I serve customers and organise the shelves. You have to be quite good with people and you have to stand all day. It is quite hard work but the staff are really friendly.
2. I drive a van and deliver to about twenty shops. You have to start at six and you have to be reliable. It involves a lot of driving alone, which some people like and some do not.
3. I supervise four people and organise the shifts. You have to be careful and you have to be able to say no. It is really interesting but it is harder than doing the work yourself.
Check yours against three things: is part one an activity rather than a title, does part two use have to, and does part three use quite, very or really?

grammar.title: Quite, very, really
grammar.explanation: Small words that go before an adjective and change how much. There are three and they form a scale.
grammar.rule:
THE SCALE — smallest to largest:

  quite   hard      less than very
  very    hard
  really  hard      more than very

WORD ORDER never changes:
  degree word + adjective
     really interesting     NOT  interesting really
     quite difficult
     very tired

ONE WARNING ABOUT QUITE:
  Here, quite = fairly. Quite good is a
  SMALLER claim than very good.
  Some speakers use quite to mean completely,
  especially with right and finished.
  Recognise that use. You do not need to
  produce it.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say a job is difficult, but not extremely so.
1. Choose the adjective: difficult.
2. Choose the amount. Not extreme, so not really. More than nothing, so not plain difficult.
3. Quite sits below very, so: It is quite difficult.
Now the same sentence at each level, so you can hear the scale:
  It is quite difficult.   fairly difficult
  It is very difficult.
  It is really difficult.  more than very
And the word order test: the degree word always comes immediately before the adjective. It is difficult really is wrong in the same way that a red big car is wrong — the order is fixed even though the meaning is guessable.
grammar.mistake: Putting the degree word after the adjective — it is interesting really. Also using quite when you mean very: quite good sounds like faint praise, and if you meant to compliment someone you have just slightly disappointed them. That is not a grammar error, but it is a real one.
grammar.tip: Quite is below very. Really is above it. All three go before the adjective.
grammar.practice:
Put the words in the right order, then say whether it is more or less than very.
1. hard / quite / it is / work
2. good / the team / really / is
3. is / interesting / quite / it
4. tired / really / I am
5. is / careful / very / she
6. Rewrite number 1 so it means more than very.
grammar.answers:
1. It is quite hard work. — less than very
2. The team is really good. — more than very
3. It is quite interesting. — less than very
4. I am really tired. — more than very
5. She is very careful. — very
6. It is really hard work.
Every answer has the degree word immediately before the adjective, which is the only word-order rule on this card.
If number 3 sounded like praise to you, that is the quite trap: it is fairly interesting, which is a smaller claim than very interesting.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — What you have to do
speaking.instructions:
Say six sentences about things you have to do — at work, at home, or in your week.
Use have to four times and has to twice, by talking about somebody else for two of them.
Record them. Play back and check every one has both words: have and to.
speaking.tutor: Say six things you have to do and ask the tutor to correct any missing to.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Not necessary
speaking.instructions:
Say six sentences using do not have to or does not have to.
After each one, say out loud what it means: that is not necessary.
For example: You do not have to have experience. That is not necessary.
Record it. The second half of each pair is there to build the habit of reading these as open doors, and it is worth saying aloud even though it feels repetitive.
speaking.tutor: Say six do-not-have-to sentences and ask the tutor whether each one forbids anything. The answer should be no every time.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Asking what is required
speaking.instructions:
Say each of these five times, until they arrive without assembly.
Do I have to work at weekends?
Do I have to have a qualification?
How much notice do I have to give?
What do I have to bring to the interview?
Does everyone have to do overtime?
Record the last two. Both are questions people wish they had asked earlier.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor five questions about what a job requires, and ask it to answer only what you asked.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — A job in three parts
speaking.instructions:
Choose a job — yours, one you have done, or one you would like.
Describe it in three parts: what you do, what it requires, what it is like.
Use have to at least twice and a degree word at least twice.
Include one sentence with involves.
Record it.
Then listen back and ask: could somebody hearing only this tell whether they could do the job, and whether they would want to? If not, one of the three parts is missing or too short.
speaking.tutor: Describe a job to the tutor and ask it which of the three parts was weakest.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — The scale
speaking.instructions:
Take one adjective — hard.
Say: It is quite hard. It is very hard. It is really hard.
Say them in order, then out of order, then ask yourself which was which.
Do the same with: interesting, difficult, busy, tired, good.
Record one full set. Listening back to your own voice on a scale is the fastest way to fix the order of the three.
speaking.tutor: Say sentences at different points on the scale and ask the tutor to rank them.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the contract aloud and decide
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read the advertisement aloud, then clauses 3.2, 4.2 and 6.1 of the contract.
Then say aloud, as though explaining to a friend: whether overtime is required, whether it is paid extra, and whether you could take a holiday in December.
Then say what the advertisement promised that the contract does not explain.
Record the last two parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor the contract clauses and ask which one it would want changed before signing.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A job described in three parts
writing.prompt:
Describe a job in three paragraphs, one for each part.
Paragraph 1: what you actually do. At least three activities.
Paragraph 2: what the job requires. At least three sentences with have to.
Paragraph 3: what it is like. Use quite, very and really at least once each, and one sentence with involves.
Then underline every have to.
writing.model:
I work in a warehouse. I organise the deliveries when they arrive, I check them against the list, and I put them where they belong. On Saturdays I also serve at the counter, because we are short of staff.
You have to start at six, which is the hardest part. You have to be reliable, because if one person does not come the whole shift is slower. You have to be careful with the heavy things, and you have to ask for help rather than trying to lift them alone.
It is quite hard work, especially in the first week. The team is really good, and that matters more than I expected. The job involves a lot of walking — about twelve kilometres a day, somebody measured it once. It is very tiring at first and then it is not.
writing.criteria: Three paragraphs matching the three parts; at least three have to sentences underlined; quite, very and really each used at least once; one involves sentence; paragraph 1 gives activities rather than a job title
writing.support: Write paragraph 2 first. The requirements are the easiest part to list, and once they are on the page the activities and the opinions are easier to see.
writing.extension: Rewrite paragraph 3 for somebody deciding whether to apply. What would you add, and what would you leave out?

writing.title: Writing 2 — Questions to ask before accepting
writing.prompt:
Write ten questions you would ask before accepting a job.
At least six must use do I have to or how much / how many.
Group them under three headings: the work, the hours, and the conditions.
After each question, write one line saying why it matters.
writing.model:
THE WORK
1. What does the job involve day to day? — The title tells me almost nothing.
2. Do I have to work alone or in a team? — This decides whether I would enjoy it.
3. Do I have to have a qualification? — If not, I can apply now rather than later.

THE HOURS
4. How many hours a week is it? — The advertisement says 30, but I want it confirmed.
5. Do I have to do overtime? — May be required is not the same as optional.
6. Is overtime paid at a higher rate? — Sometimes it is not, and that changes the pay a lot.
7. Do I have to work weekends? — I need to know before I agree, not after.

THE CONDITIONS
8. How much holiday do I get? — And whether public holidays are included.
9. Do I have to give notice, and how much? — It is in the contract and it changes after three months.
10. Is there a trial period? — If so, either side can end it quickly, and I should know that.
writing.length: Ten questions under three headings, each with a reason
writing.criteria: Ten questions; at least six using do I have to or a how much / how many form; three headings; every question followed by a reason that says why it matters to you specifically
writing.support: Write the reasons first if the questions do not come. Start from what would annoy you six months into a job you did not ask about, and the question writes itself.
writing.extension: Mark the three you would ask at an interview and the three you would wait and ask after being offered the job. The order matters more than people expect.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the advertisement and the contract
writing.prompt:
Use the advertisement and contract in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. The advertisement says no experience necessary. What does that mean, and should you apply if you have none?
2. Do you have to do overtime, and is it paid at a higher rate?
3. You want a week off in December. Can you?
4. You leave after two months. How much notice, and why is that different from later?
5. Name one thing the advertisement promises that the contract does not explain, and say what you would ask.
writing.model:
1. It means experience is not required, so I should apply. It is an open door, not a warning.
2. Yes — clause 3.2 says employees may be required to work up to 8 hours a week, so it is not optional. It is paid at the normal hourly rate, not a higher one.
3. No. Clause 4.2 says holiday may not be taken during November or December.
4. One week, because the first three months are a trial period under clause 6.2. After three months the notice period becomes four weeks.
5. The advertisement promises a free staff bus from the station, but nothing says what times it runs. I would ask whether it runs early enough for a shift starting at six, because if it does not, the promise is worth nothing to me.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 gives both facts from clause 3.2; answer 4 cites the trial period; answer 5 identifies a genuine gap rather than a detail
writing.support: Read the advertisement and the contract as two separate documents that disagree in tone. The advertisement is selling; the contract is binding. Every question here is answered by the contract.
writing.extension: Rewrite the advertisement so that it is still attractive but nothing in it would surprise someone who later reads the contract.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. I have start at eight.
2. She have to wear a uniform.
3. Do you has to work weekends?
4. You do not have to wear a uniform, so uniforms are forbidden.
5. It is interesting really.
6. The job is quite good — better than very good.
7. I am a driver. (you have been asked to describe the job)
8. He do not have to give notice.
writing.model:
1. I have to start at eight. (Pattern 1 — have to is two words)
2. She has to wear a uniform. (Pattern 1 — third person takes has)
3. Do you have to work weekends? (Pattern 1 — after do, the verb is plain: have, not has)
4. You do not have to wear a uniform, so a uniform is not required. (Pattern 1 — do not have to means not necessary, never forbidden)
5. It is really interesting. (Pattern 3 — the degree word goes before the adjective)
6. The job is quite good — but that is less than very good. (Pattern 3 — quite sits below very, not above)
7. I serve customers and organise the deliveries. You have to be reliable. It is quite hard work but really interesting. (Pattern 2 — a description has three parts, not a title)
8. He does not have to give notice. (Pattern 1 — third person takes does in the negative)
writing.criteria: All eight corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; number 4 corrects the meaning rather than the grammar; number 7 supplies all three parts
writing.support: Numbers 1, 2, 3 and 8 are all the same pattern going wrong in four different places: the to, the third-person s, the verb after do, and the negative. Fix them as a set and the pattern is secure.
writing.extension: Number 4 is the only one where the grammar was already correct and the meaning was wrong. Write two more like it.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Have to, has to, do not have to
activities.instructions:
Write the right form.
1. I ____ start at eight every day.
2. She ____ wear a uniform — it is a rule.
3. You ____ have experience. Anyone can apply.
4. He ____ give four weeks' notice.
5. We ____ work weekends. It is optional.
6. ____ I ____ bring anything to the interview?
7. Everyone ____ read the contract before signing.
8. She ____ pay for the training. The employer pays.
9. ____ he ____ work overtime?
10. New staff ____ be supervised for the first month.
11. You ____ have your own transport. There is a staff bus.
12. The employer ____ give you a contract in writing.
activities.answers:
1. have to  2. has to  3. do not have to  4. has to  5. do not have to  6. Do … have to  7. has to  8. does not have to  9. Does … have to  10. have to  11. do not have to  12. has to
The four negatives — 3, 5, 8 and 11 — all mean the same thing: it is not necessary. None of them forbids anything. Read each one again and say aloud what is now allowed.
Number 7 uses has to because everyone is third person singular, which surprises people. Everyone, somebody and nobody all take the -s form.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Required, or not required?
activities.instructions:
For each sentence, write REQUIRED or NOT REQUIRED. Then write one line saying what the person can actually do.
1. You have to wear safety shoes.
2. You do not have to have experience.
3. Everyone has to sign in at the gate.
4. You do not have to work weekends.
5. She has to give four weeks' notice.
6. You do not have to have your own transport.
7. All staff have to attend the training.
8. You do not have to have a qualification.
9. He has to start at six.
10. You do not have to do overtime.
activities.answers:
REQUIRED: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
NOT REQUIRED: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
What the person can do, for the NOT REQUIRED ones:
2. Apply without experience.
4. Work weekdays only — or work weekends if they want the extra hours.
6. Take the staff bus, or drive if they prefer.
8. Apply without a qualification.
10. Say no to overtime.
That second column is the point of the exercise. Every one of the five is something the person is now free to do, and if any of your lines said cannot or must not, read the sentence again.

activities.title: Practice 3 — How much?
activities.instructions:
Choose quite, very or really so the sentence matches the meaning in brackets.
1. It is ____ hard. (fairly hard, not extremely)
2. The team is ____ good. (more than very)
3. I am ____ tired. (more than very)
4. It is ____ interesting. (fairly)
5. She is ____ careful. (a large amount, standard word)
6. The pay is ____ low. (more than very)
7. It is ____ far from where I live. (fairly)
8. The first week was ____ difficult. (more than very)
activities.answers:
1. quite  2. really  3. really  4. quite  5. very  6. really  7. quite  8. really
The scale is quite, then very, then really. If you put very where really belongs the sentence is still correct English — it just makes a smaller claim than you meant.
Check the word order in every answer: the degree word comes immediately before the adjective, with nothing between them.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Describe four jobs
activities.instructions:
Describe each job in three parts — what you do, what it requires, what it is like. One sentence per part.
1. Working in a shop.
2. Driving a delivery van.
3. Supervising a small team.
4. Repairing machines.
5. A job you have done.
6. A job you would like to do.
activities.answers:
Model answers for 1 to 4 — yours will differ, and should.
1. I serve customers and organise the shelves. You have to be quite good with people and you have to stand all day. It is hard work but the staff are really friendly.
2. I drive a van and deliver to about twenty shops. You have to start at six and you have to be reliable. It involves a lot of driving alone.
3. I supervise four people and organise the shifts. You have to be careful and you have to be able to say no. It is really interesting but harder than doing the work yourself.
4. I repair machines when they break down. You have to be careful and you have to work quickly, because nothing is running while you work. It is quite satisfying, because you can see what you have done.
Check each of yours against three things: part one is an activity not a title, part two uses have to, part three uses a degree word.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Read a real job advertisement
activities.instructions:
Find one real job advertisement — in a window, a newspaper, or online.
Write down: what the job involves, three things it requires, and anything it says is not required.
Then write down two things the advertisement does not tell you that you would want to know.
Bring the list to your next session, or keep it with your work.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your advertisement.
What most people find: the requirements are listed clearly and the conditions are not. Pay is often given as a range or left out, hours are given as about, and nothing says whether overtime is required.
The second finding is that at least one not required line is in there somewhere — no experience necessary, or training given. Those lines are written to bring people in, and they mean exactly what they say.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Describe a job to somebody else
activities.instructions:
This week, ask somebody about their job and listen for the three parts.
Write down: what they said they do, what they said it requires, and what they said it is like.
Then note which of the three they gave first, and which they left out until you asked.
activities.answers:
No key.
What almost everybody finds: people give the title first and the activities only when asked a second question. Most leave out what it requires entirely, because it is obvious to them and invisible to you.
The third part — what it is like — usually comes last and is usually the longest, once it starts. If you get only one part, ask what does that actually involve day to day, and the rest follows.

quizzes.q: You do not have to have experience. What does this mean?
options: Experience is forbidden
Experience is not required
You should not mention experience
Experience is essential
quizzes.why: Do not have to means it is not necessary. It never means something is forbidden — it is an open door, and in a job advertisement it is an invitation to apply.

options: She have to wear a uniform.
She has to wear a uniform.
She has wear a uniform.
She have wear a uniform.
quizzes.a: She has to wear a uniform.
quizzes.why: Third person takes has, and have to is two words — both parts are needed.

options: Do you have to work weekends?
Do you has to work weekends?
Have you to work weekends?
You have to work weekends?
quizzes.a: Do you have to work weekends?
quizzes.why: Have is an ordinary verb here, so the question uses do, and the verb after do stays plain — have, not has.

quizzes.q: Which sentence means the smallest amount?
options: It is really hard.
It is very hard.
It is quite hard.
They are all the same.
quizzes.why: The scale runs quite, very, really. Quite means fairly, which is a smaller claim than very — so quite good is faint praise, not high praise.

options: It is really interesting.
It is interesting really.
Really it is interesting job.
It is interesting very.
quizzes.why: The degree word goes immediately before the adjective, with nothing between them. The order is fixed even though the meaning would be guessable either way.

quizzes.q: What are the three parts of a job description?
options: The title, the pay and the hours
What you do, what it requires, what it is like
The employer, the contract and the notice
Your experience, your qualifications and your references
quizzes.a: What you do, what it requires, what it is like
quizzes.why: Each answers a different question. Without the second, nobody can judge whether they could do it; without the third, it sounds like a contract rather than a life.

quizzes.q: Which sentence uses have to correctly?
options: I have start at six.
I having to start at six.
I has to start at six.
I have to start at six.
quizzes.a: I have to start at six.
quizzes.why: First person takes have, and to is required. The most common error at this level is dropping the to entirely.

quizzes.q: What does the verb involves mean?
options: Includes as a necessary part
Is forbidden by
Is paid extra for
Happens occasionally
quizzes.why: It lets you state a fact about the work that is neither a duty nor an opinion — the job involves a lot of walking is exactly the thing a listener most wants to know.

quizzes.q: The contract says overtime may be required and is paid at the normal hourly rate. What does this tell you?
options: Overtime is optional and paid extra
You must do overtime and it is paid extra
You may have to do overtime and it is not paid extra
There is no overtime in this job
quizzes.a: You may have to do overtime and it is not paid extra
quizzes.why: Two facts sit in one clause, and the second is the one that costs money. Overtime is often paid at a higher rate; this contract says it is not.

quizzes.q: Which of these is NOT a prohibition?
options: Staff must not enter this area.
Holiday may not be taken in December.
No smoking beyond this point.
You do not have to work weekends.
quizzes.a: You do not have to work weekends.
quizzes.why: It is the only open door in the list. The other three close something; this one says weekends are optional, so the person may work them if they want the hours.

options: He does not have to give notice.
He do not have to give notice.
He does not have give notice.
He not have to give notice.
quizzes.a: He does not have to give notice.
quizzes.why: Third person takes does in the negative, and the to stays. Both parts go wrong independently, which is why this form is worth drilling.

quizzes.q: The contract says the first 3 months are a trial period with 1 week's notice. What does that mean for you?
options: You cannot leave for three months
You are paid less for three months
You have no contract for three months
Either side can end it with one week's notice
quizzes.a: Either side can end it with one week's notice
quizzes.why: The short notice cuts both ways — it is easier for you to leave and easier for the employer to end it. Clause 6.2 says so explicitly.

teacherNotes.note: Three pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key. Practice 2 is the diagnostic and it is built in two columns on purpose: sorting REQUIRED from NOT REQUIRED is the easy half, and writing what the person can now actually do is the half that reveals whether the meaning has landed. A learner who writes cannot in that column has not understood, and the answer key says so directly.

teacherNotes.type: The one thing that must not be got wrong
teacherNotes.note: Do not have to reads as a prohibition to a large proportion of learners, and the cost is not an exercise mark — it is a job advertisement misread and not applied to. Reading 1 exists solely for this. The unit deliberately contains no prohibition form at all, so that every negative a learner meets here is an open door; must and mustn't are held back to Unit 17.

teacherNotes.type: Almost nothing here is new grammar
teacherNotes.note: Third-person -s is Unit 3, the present simple is Unit 5, and do and does in questions and negatives is Unit 5. What is new is one verb pattern and the meaning of its negative. If a learner struggles with does not have to, check whether the problem is the modal meaning or just the third-person does — they are different problems and the second is a Unit 5 review.

teacherNotes.type: Quite is genuinely ambiguous and we teach only one use
teacherNotes.note: Quite means fairly in this course, and the card says plainly that some speakers use it to mean completely with words like right and finished. Learners will meet that use and should recognise it without being asked to produce it. Teaching both productively at A2 causes more errors than it prevents.

teacherNotes.type: Why the advertisement and the contract together
teacherNotes.note: Neither document is dishonest and they say different things. The advertisement offers a free staff bus; the contract never mentions it, and no document states the times — which is the gap question in Reading 3 and Writing 3. Four of the ten comprehension questions need the contract rather than the advertisement, which is the practical lesson: the conditions that affect you are in the document you sign, not the one that attracted you.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Practice 5 asks learners to work from a real job advertisement and Practice 6 to ask a real person about their job: neither the advertisement, the employer's name, nor anything the other person said should be collected, shared or entered into the app. Practice 6 asks only for the shape of what was said, not the content, and that wording should stay.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what I have to do at work, and ask whether something is required.
I can tell the difference between something that is not required and something that is not allowed.
I can describe a job, including what it requires and what it is like to do.
I can say quite hard, very hard and really hard and mean three different amounts.

assignment.title: A job described, and a contract read
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record a full three-part description of a job — what you do, what it requires, what it is like — using have to at least twice, a degree word at least twice, and one sentence with involves; then listen back and record one further sentence saying which of the three parts was weakest and why. Second, write full-sentence answers to the five situations in Writing 3, using the advertisement and contract in Reading 3, and add a sixth thing you would want confirmed in writing before signing, with the question you would ask. Keep both together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written answers
